title: FAIR Clinics: from principles to practice
content:
"Join us for our half-day event focused on bringing FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) practices to everyday medical research.

This year marks 10 years since the introduction of the FAIR principles. Over the past decade, much has been achieved - but for many researchers, FAIR can still feel abstract and difficult to translate into daily practice. Many recognize its importance but continue to face a simple question Where do I start?

This event is designed to answer exactly that!

We introduce FAIR Clinics - short, hands-on sessions where you will actively work on concrete outputs relevant to your research. The attention is not just on why FAIR matters, but on how to get started in practice."

title: Motivation and concerns regarding the use of preprints among Brazilian health researchers: a survey | medRxiv
content: Abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the motivations and concerns related to preprint use among Brazilian health researchers. A mixed-methods online survey of all 1,596 holders of CNPq Research Productivity Grants in seven health fields was conducted in 2025. The questionnaire was adapted from a survey of bioRxiv authors, translated into Portuguese, and pilot-tested. Closed-ended responses were analyzed descriptively, and free-text responses were grouped by similarity. Overall, 178 researchers accessed the survey (11.2%), and 143 answered items on preprints and were included in the final analysis (9.0% effective response rate). The mean age was 55.9 years, and 88.0% were affiliated with public institutions. Regarding corresponding-author publications over the previous five years, 62.2% of respondents had deposited no preprints, while 37.8% had deposited at least one. Among preprints users, 79.2% agreed that deposition was freely decided by the authors. The main motivations were rapid sharing of findings (69.8%) and obtaining feedback (49.1%). title: Managing versions in a Publish-Review-Curate ecosystem A landscape review and request for comments
content: "Participating in Publish-Review-Curate publishing requires that "Publish" infrastructures - repositories and preprint servers - provide robust version support, since this is required to ensure coherence in the PRC landscape. After a review of current practices, we are asking for feedback from PRC practitioners and repositories about the practices we have identified, what works best from your perspective, and whether we have missed anything important. Please provide your comments directly in this google document or by sending them to kathleen.shearer@coar-repositories.org by the end of September."

title: Personal Research Ontologies for Personal Open Science | Proceedings of the 14th ACM Collective Intelligence Conference
content: Abstract: As researchers conduct their work, they incrementally construct a personal research ontology: a rich, personal understanding of their field and its phenomena. Yet most of this knowledge remains internalized, with only fragments surfacing in publications. This position paper argues that research is fundamentally an act of personal ontology construction and proposes Personal Open Science (POS), a lightweight method for externalizing a researcher’s personal research ontology for downstream use. The method requires no machine learning or language models, and it centers on the researcher rather than on the publication, the traditional focal unit of Open Science. Building on daily reading habits and a minimal annotation scheme, the approach adds little overhead while producing a structured, explorable representation of a researcher’s interests, influences, and expertise. I demonstrate the method through my own practice of annotating over 45,000 documents across a decade of research. title: We Must Open the Frontier: OSI, OFAI Support Calls for the U.S. to Develop More Open Models – Open Source Initiative
content:
"The Open Source Initiative joins the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) in supporting calls for the U.S. to develop more open models because they promote competition in AI through local control and lower costs. The OFAI is a university-led, collaborative initiative that aims to bend the arc toward human-centered, responsible, transparent, and ethical AI. Led by Carnegie Mellon University, the OFAI includes university representatives from across the country as well as nonprofit voices and individual fellows from industry and government. As the policy lead, we collaborated with other OFAI members to lay out the benefits of Open Source AI and open-weight models in comparison to closed, proprietary ones. 

The statement asserts that the U.S. needs more “focus, investment, and collaboration from the full breadth of the innovation pipeline to accelerate the development of open models. This will require a strategic approach that moves beyond the status quo, bringing together new partners, both technical and non-technical, from across industry, academia, and government.” ..."

title: Open Access in the European Research Area: progress remains uneven as new report calls for more concerted action - Research and innovation
content:
"A new independent expert report published today by the European Commission highlights that, despite notable advancement, the implementation of open access across the European Research Area remains uneven and fragmented. While progress has been made, persistent barriers continue to hinder widespread open access, and further action is needed.

Over the past decade, European Union soft-law measures, national strategies, funder mandates, and, where applicable, national legislation have advanced open access. However, these efforts have not yet produced a coherent framework across the European Research Area, leaving researchers, institutions, and funders to navigate differing policies.

The report provides a snapshot of the current open access landscape, offering policy recommendations to improve access to scientific publications and research data. It draws on an analysis of all 27 EU Member States and eight non-EU countries."

title: Reframing Repositories – COAR
content:
"Scholarly communication is at a crossroads. Scholarly infrastructure has become dangerously concentrated in the hands of a small number of commercial publishers and foreign-controlled platforms, leaving institutions and nations exposed to disruptions they cannot control.

At the same time, the integrity of the scientific record is under acute strain, as AI-generated fabrications, paper mills, and reproducibility failures erode the trust on which science depends and public trust in information is fragile, at precisely the moment when citizens most need reliable access to evidence. Repositories help to address all of these challenges.

To highlight the critical importance of repositories, COAR is publishing a “Narrative Series”. The series provides several compelling, evidence-based portrayals that, taken together, build a powerful case for repositories as essential infrastructure for scholarly communications and the global knowledge commons."

title: Open as Antidote – addressing the big challenges facing science
content:
"This course, called Open as Antidote – addressing the big challenges facing science, was part of the 2026 FORCE11 Scholarly Communication Institute which ran with the theme of ‘FSCI2026: Critical Thinking and evolving open scholarship in the era of AI’

These blog posts are a series of ‘explainer’ pre-reading to start participants thinking about the issues the course considered in relation to the general decline of scholarly publishing. The blog posts in this series considered the problem of questionable research practices, the mechanisms to manage these through corrections and retractions, the problem of university rankings and the uneasy nexus between Open and AI. They finish with some suggestions of where we go from here."
